chapter_theme: Holding one's own close: the sympathy of kin dissolves suffering, the worthy bear everyone who leans on them without sorting people into ours and others, and plain food from those who love is sweeter than a feast from those who don't. The bond is proved when it goes into the fire with you.
structure_note: 201 to 205 concern the comfort kin give and the duty of the worthy to bear all who come; 206, 207 and 210 make one point three times through food; 208 and 209 test the bond by adversity. The verses move between kin (கேளிர், கிளைஞர், தமர்) and intimates (நட்டார்), and Mudaliar glosses நட்டார் as kin.

201.reading: As a mother forgets the cravings of pregnancy, the strain of carrying and the pain of birth when she sees her son on her lap, the trouble a person has suffered through weakness vanishes when he sees kin who ask after him.
201.nuance: The kin do nothing but come and ask how he is (உசாவுதல்). The comfort the verse describes lies in being asked after, not in material help.

202.reading: The duty of a good man is to shelter all who come to him alike, as a shade tree does in fierce heat, and to toil himself so that many enjoy what he yields, as a fruiting tree does.
202.nuance: தான் வருந்தி makes the giver's own hardship part of the duty rather than a cost to avoid. Mudaliar takes பழுமரம் as the banyan and notes that others read it as a ripe fruiting tree, as Shanmuganar and Pope do.

203.reading: Lord of the land of piled-up hills, the great never say 'we will not support' those who have come to depend on them; is there any branch that cannot bear its own fruit, however many and heavy they hang?
203.nuance: The image makes dependants the supporter's own fruit, so bearing them is part of his nature rather than an act of charity.

204.reading: The friendship of small-natured people does not last beyond a few days, even when they mingle so fully that the world knows it; the bond with those who never falter holds as steadily as the ascetics who keep to their path to the goal.
204.nuance: Both commentators read the comparison as ascetics who never leave the discipline of renunciation, and Mudaliar names the goal as release (வீடு). Pope's translation makes the line say how long the bond lasts, which is less clear in the Tamil.

205.reading: Those fit to be counted chief among men have no trace of the talk that sorts people as 'of this kind, so many, ours, others', and they draw near and relieve the distress of anyone who is perishing.
205.nuance: In a chapter on embracing kin, this verse removes the boundary of kinship: for the best people, anyone in distress counts as their own. Mudaliar glosses எமர் and பிறர் as those we want and those we don't.

206.reading: Saltless millet gruel in any vessel, taken among kin as dear as life, is always sweeter than rice white as a tiger's claw, served with sugar and milk in a golden dish from the hands of those who are not one's own.
206.nuance: The contrast is total on every count, the vessel, the grain, the salt and the giver, and only the giver decides the taste.

207.reading: A hot fried feast given as hospitality at the proper hour in the house of those not close to one is bitter as neem; greens served at an untimely afternoon hour are sweet when they come from one's own people.
207.nuance: Even the hour is reversed: the stranger's meal is punctual and the kin's is late, and the kin's is still the sweeter.

208.reading: Those who pound at you every day like a hammer, eating off you, let go like tongs when the fire comes; those rightly called intimates enter the fire with you like the smith's poker.
208.nuance: The three smithy tools sort people by how they behave in the heat. Mudaliar offers two readings of முனியாது, 'without tiring' or 'showing affection', and of கொட்டி, 'striking' or 'pestering'. Pope's translation is missing for this quatrain.

positions.position: Those who enter the fire are loving kin.
Those who enter the fire are true friends.
positions.quote: உண்மை நண்பர் எனப்படுவார், பொருளோடு நெருப்பிலே நிற்கும் உலையாணிக்கோல் போல

209.reading: Maiden with the cool garland of fragrant flowers, if friends share their friends' joys until death but not their sorrows, is there anything they could do for them even in the next world?
209.nuance: The claim is negative: sharing only joys makes no bond at all. Mudaliar again glosses நட்டார் as kin, where Shanmuganar has friends. The verse is addressed to a woman, which Mudaliar notes.

210.reading: A hot fried dish the colour of a cat's eye, eaten sitting apart in the house of those without affection, is bitter as neem; watery cold gruel in the house of loving equals is ambrosia that joins with one's bones.
210.nuance: வேறிருந்து, sitting apart, names the slight: the food is served but the guest is kept separate.

links.note: 521 says that only kin keep honouring old ties when a man has lost everything; 201 describes what that loyalty does inside the sufferer, likening it to a mother forgetting the pains of birth.
Both make the good man a fruiting tree that the many enjoy. 216 says his wealth is like a tree ripening in the middle of town; 202 adds the shade tree and insists he toils for it himself.
Both put the burden of those who depend on a household on its capable members: 1027 compares them to the brave in battle, 203 to a branch that never fails to bear its own fruit.
Both contrast a friendship that holds or grows with one that soon fails; 782 uses the waxing and waning moon, 204 the ascetic's unswerving path.

Both distrust speech that labels a relation, and their wording is close (இனையர், இன்னர்/இன்னம்). 790 says friendship looks shabby when friends describe what they are to each other; 205 says the best people never sort others into ours and theirs.

Both say that plain gruel (கூழ், புற்கை) shared with one's own is sweeter than the finest food. The Kural says it is sweeter than ambrosia when one's children's little hands have stirred it; 206 says it is sweeter than a golden-dish feast from those who are not one's own.
The kin chapter and the chapter on testing friendship use the same contrast of poor food given with love and rich food given without it. 217 ends in the bitter strychnos fruit, 206 and 210 in neem.

Both say that hospitality without warmth spoils the meal for the guest. 90 says a guest withers like the anicham flower at an averted face; 207 says the punctual feast in an unloving house tastes of neem.
Both single out those who leave when ruin comes: 208 compares them to tongs that let go in the fire, and 799 says the memory of such friends burns the heart at the hour of death.
787 defines friendship partly as sharing the suffering in ruin; 209 says a friendship that shares only joys can do nothing even in the next world.
